screens.title: Building and Testing with AWS CodeBuild
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson we focus on AWS CodeBuild as a managed continuous integration service that compiles code, runs tests, and produces deployable artifacts. You will learn why designing the right build environment matters, how the buildspec. yml file controls each phase, and practical ways to speed up builds using caching and appropriate compute types. We will also show how CodeBuild fits into an automated pipeline and how to use CloudWatch logs and the service role to diagnose failures. A concrete example in this chapter walks through creating a simple Node. js project, adding a buildspec with caching for npm packages, running a build, then running it again to observe cache restoration. Along the way we call out common mistakes, such as using oversized base images or missing IAM permissions, and how to resolve them. By the end you should be able to choose between managed images or custom Docker images, author purposeful buildspec phases, and interpret logs to fix failing builds. Think about a recent build you ran slowly: which of the ideas here could speed it up or make failures easier to fix?

Building and Testing with AWS CodeBuild

Design custom build environments, author effective buildspecs, and make builds fast, repeatable, and secure. Practical Node.js example and logs-based troubleshooting included.

In this lesson
Build environments, buildspec phases, caching, compute, pipelines, and logs.

Faster builds and clearer logs let teams ship safer software more often while controlling cost.

Artifacts & Cache: S3 or local; CloudWatch logs for troubleshooting

Custom Docker environments

buildspec.yml

screens.title: What is AWS CodeBuild?
screens.narratorSegment: AWS CodeBuild is a fully managed continuous integration service that compiles source code, runs tests, and produces artifacts ready for deployment. The core claim is that CodeBuild removes the need to provision and manage your own build servers by offering on-demand build capacity that scales automatically, so you pay only for build minutes consumed. A concrete example: a repository push triggers a pipeline, CodeBuild pulls the source, runs install commands, executes unit tests, and zips artifacts to S3 for later deployment. A common misconception is that CodeBuild alone handles orchestration; in practice, you typically integrate it into CodePipeline or other orchestrators to form a CI/CD workflow. Another misunderstanding is assuming every managed image contains every tool; you may need to install or supply a custom image for specialized tools. Key takeaway: CodeBuild handles execution and scaling, but you must define the commands, artifacts, and environment so that builds are reproducible and secure. Ask yourself: which repeating manual steps in your current builds could be codified into a buildspec so they run automatically every time? What is AWS CodeBuild? means codebuild runs builds in managed or custom environments, scaling compute and producing artifacts while you pay for build time only.. In practical terms, a managed ci service that runs builds and produces artifacts. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.2 › What is AWS CodeBuild?
Core definition

CodeBuild compiles source code, runs tests, and generates artifacts. It provides on-demand compute and avoids managing build servers.

Analogy
Think of CodeBuild like a rental build machine you script: you provide the recipe, and CodeBuild runs it, scales as needed, then returns the output.
Common misconception
It is not an orchestrator by itself. Use CodePipeline or other tools to coordinate stages.
Quick scenario
A push to your repository triggers a pipeline. CodeBuild checks out the code, runs install and build commands defined in buildspec.yml, executes tests, and places the artifact in S3 for deployment.
Key takeaway
Key Takeaway

CodeBuild automates builds at scale; you must provide the build recipe and environment to make builds reproducible and secure.

screens.title: Build Environments: managed images vs custom Docker
screens.narratorSegment: Choosing the right build environment is a practical trade-off. CodeBuild offers managed images for common runtimes like Node. js, Java, Python, and Docker, which simplify setup for standard projects. However, advanced projects often require pre-installed tools, specific compilers, or proprietary software; for those you provide a custom Docker image stored in Amazon ECR or Docker Hub. Custom images let you guarantee tool versions and reduce repeated install steps, but you must keep images lean to avoid longer startup times. A common mistake is using a large base image with unnecessary packages; prefer smaller bases such as slim or Alpine where feasible. Security matters: regularly scan custom images and build them from trusted sources. Example: if your build runs a proprietary static analysis tool, bake it into a custom image and push to ECR so CodeBuild can pull it during the build without additional install steps. Misconception to avoid: assume managed images include every build tool; always verify the managed image documentation and install missing tools in the install phase or via a custom image. How would you balance startup time and reproducibility in your project?

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.2 › Build Environments
Managed images

Provide common runtimes quickly for Java, Node.js, Python, Go, .NET, and Docker. They minimize setup but may not contain every build tool your project needs.

When to use custom Docker
  • Pre-install proprietary tools, compilers, or exact tool versions.
  • Remove repeated install time by baking dependencies into the image.
  • Store the image in ECR and reference it from CodeBuild.
Security note
Scan custom images for vulnerabilities and build from trusted base images to reduce risk.
Architecture sketch
Managed image: Quick start, no image maintenance.
Custom image in ECR: preinstalled tools, reproducible environment.
Trade-off: image size affects startup time; keep images lean.
Key takeaway
Key Takeaway

Choose managed images for convenience and custom images for control, optimizing image size to reduce build startup time.

screens.title: Understanding buildspec.yml
screens.narratorSegment: The buildspec. yml file is the heart of a CodeBuild project. It is a YAML document typically stored at the root of your repository that instructs CodeBuild what to do during each phase. The main phases are install for dependency installation, pre_build for checks like linting or security scans, build for compiling and unit tests, and post_build for packaging artifacts or pushing Docker images. You can also define artifacts to collect build outputs and cache. paths to persist dependency caches. A concrete example is a Node. js project that sets runtime-versions: nodejs: 18 in install and runs npm install, then runs tests in build and zips artifacts in post_build. A common mistake is incorrect paths in cache. paths or artifacts. base-directory, causing caches to miss or artifacts to be empty. When a build fails because a tool is missing, ensure the managed image supports the runtime or add installation commands to the install phase, or use a custom image. Close by asking: does your buildspec clearly separate environment setup from build steps so failures are easier to diagnose? Understanding buildspec.yml means author structured phases and declare artifacts and cache paths to make builds deterministic and fast.. In practical terms, phases, commands, artifacts, and cache. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.2 › Understanding buildspec.yml
Phases explained
  • install: configure runtimes and install dependencies.
  • pre_build: static analysis, linting, or security scans.
  • build: compile code and run unit tests.
  • post_build: package artifacts or push images.
Common pitfall
Incorrect cache or artifact paths lead to missing cache restores or empty artifacts. Verify base-directory and cache.paths carefully.
Example snippet
version: 0.2
phases:
  install:
    runtime-versions:
      nodejs: 18
    commands:
      - echo "Installing dependencies..."
      - npm install
  pre_build:
    commands:
      - echo "Running linting and security checks..."
      - npm run lint
  build:
    commands:
      - echo "Building application..."
      - npm run build
      - echo "Running unit tests..."
      - npm test
  post_build:
    commands:
      - echo "Packaging artifacts..."
artifacts:
  files:
    - '**/*'
  base-directory: 'build'
cache:
  paths:
    - '/root/.npm/**/*'
This snippet shows install through post_build, artifacts base-directory, and an S3-local cache path for npm packages.

screens.title: Example buildspec for Node.js
screens.narratorSegment: Here we walk through the example buildspec. yml used for the Node. js hands-on activity. The file locks runtime-versions to nodejs: 18 in the install phase and runs npm install to restore dependencies. The build phase runs the build script and unit tests, while the post_build phase packages artifacts, such as zipping the app for S3 storage. Notice cache. paths includes /root/. npm so subsequent builds can restore node_modules from S3 and avoid downloading packages again. A practical mistake to watch for is using an incorrect cache path format; the pattern '/root/. npm/**/*' captures nested files and is commonly recommended. If caches are not found, check the CodeBuild project's cache configuration in the console, ensure the service role has s3:GetObject and s3:PutObject permissions, and confirm the bucket and prefix names match. This example is intentionally simple so you can run it, observe logs like "Restoring cache...", and then experiment by changing the cache path and re-running builds to see the effect. content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.2 › Example buildspec for Node.js
Why this example works
  • Runtime version ensures node behavior is consistent across builds.
  • Separate phases make failures easier to locate: install vs build vs post_build.
  • Cache path for npm reduces install time when restored.
Troubleshooting hint
If you see "Cache not found" check IAM permissions and that the build project cache configuration points to the correct S3 bucket and prefix.
buildspec.yml (copyable)
version: 0.2
phases:
  install:
    runtime-versions:
      nodejs: 18
    commands:
      - echo "Installing dependencies..."
      - npm install
  pre_build:
    commands:
      - echo "Running linting and security checks..."
      - npm run lint
  build:
    commands:
      - echo "Building application..."
      - npm run build
      - echo "Running unit tests..."
      - npm test
  post_build:
    commands:
      - echo "Packaging artifacts..."
      - cp -r build/* .
artifacts:
  files:
    - '**/*'
  base-directory: 'build'
cache:
  paths:
    - '/root/.npm/**/*'

screens.title: Caching strategies to speed builds
screens.narratorSegment: Caching is one of the most effective levers to reduce build times. CodeBuild supports S3 caching, which is useful for larger caches that multiple projects share, and local caching, which is faster but scoped to a single build project. A concrete example: caching the node package store at /root/. npm lets subsequent builds skip re-downloading all dependencies. To enable caching you define cache. paths in buildspec. yml and configure the CodeBuild project's cache type to S3 or Local. If you pick S3, ensure the service role has s3:GetObject and s3:PutObject permission for the cache bucket. If you see "Cache not found" in logs, likely causes are incorrect cache paths, misspelled bucket names, or insufficient IAM permissions. Test caching by running a build twice: the first run creates the cache, and the second should show "Restoring cache..." and a faster install phase. Misconception: caching always speeds builds; in some cases a corrupt or stale cache may cause failures, so add cache invalidation strategies when dependencies change dramatically. What cache strategy best fits your environment: fast local restores for a single project, or S3 to share caches across teams?

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.2 › Caching strategies
S3 caching
Best for larger caches and sharing across projects. Requires S3 bucket configuration and proper IAM permissions for the CodeBuild service role.
Local caching
Faster restores for a single project. Good for iterative development when the cache doesn't need to be shared.
Validation step
Run the build twice and watch CloudWatch logs for "Restoring cache..." to confirm correct setup.
Practical example
Add cache.paths: - '/root/.npm/**/*' to your buildspec and configure the CodeBuild project cache to S3 with a specific bucket and prefix. After the first successful build, check the S3 bucket for cache objects, then run a second build and confirm faster install times.
Common failure
If logs show "Cache not found", verify the cache path, bucket name, and that the service role has s3:GetObject and s3:PutObject permissions.

screens.title: Compute types and cost-performance trade-offs
screens.narratorSegment: CodeBuild offers a range of compute types with different C P U and memory characteristics. The right choice depends on your workload: a small static site build usually needs minimal C P U and memory and benefits from a smaller compute type, while large parallel test suites or container builds may require larger types like XLARGE. The primary trade-off is cost versus speed — oversized compute wastes money, while undersized compute can make builds slow or cause out-of-memory failures. A practical tip: profile a typical build run on a medium instance then measure whether C P U or memory is saturated; scale up only when the workload requires it. Misconception to avoid: choosing the largest compute type by default to make builds faster; this increases your bill with diminishing returns. Also consider using caching and optimizing the build steps before scaling compute. Key takeaway: match compute type to measurable needs and optimize the build process first to avoid unnecessary cost. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.2 › Compute types & cost
Trade-offs
  • Small compute: cheaper, slower for heavy builds.
  • Large compute: faster, more expensive, avoid unless needed.
  • Profile before scaling: measure CPU and memory during a build.
Practical steps
  1. Run builds on a medium compute and record runtimes and resource usage.
  2. If CPU or memory is saturated, increment compute tier and re-test.
  3. Prefer build optimizations and caching before increasing compute.
Key takeaway
Key Takeaway

screens.title: Integrating CodeBuild into CodePipeline and roles
screens.narratorSegment: CodeBuild commonly serves as a build or test action inside an AWS CodePipeline stage. The pipeline provides orchestration: a source stage hands artifacts to CodeBuild, CodeBuild produces compiled artifacts or Docker images, and subsequent stages deploy or run additional tests. Security is enforced by the CodeBuild service role — an IAM role assumed during builds. This role needs least-privilege permissions to access sources (CodeCommit, S3, GitHub), S3 buckets for artifacts and cache, ECR for Docker images, and CloudWatch Logs. A frequent troubleshooting scenario is a permission-related failure: for example, a build cannot upload artifacts to S3 because the service role lacks s3:PutObject. To resolve this, inspect CloudWatch logs for permission-denied messages and update the service role policies accordingly. Misconception: granting overly broad access to the role may seem simple but increases attack surface. Always grant just the permissions the build requires. After integrating, run a pipeline and observe that builds are triggered automatically by source changes, producing artifacts that feed the next stages. Integrating CodeBuild into CodePipeline and roles means use codepipeline to orchestrate builds; grant the codebuild service role least privilege for sources, s3, ecr, and cloudwatch logs.. screens.title: Troubleshooting CodeBuild failures
screens.narratorSegment: Troubleshooting CodeBuild builds requires a methodical approach. The primary source of truth is CloudWatch Logs, which stream every command and its output. Start by locating the timestamp where the build stopped or where an error message appears, then inspect the failing command and its exit code. Common root causes include incorrect buildspec syntax, missing tools in the environment, incorrect cache or artifact paths, network failures to external resources, and insufficient IAM permissions for the service role. For example, an "mvn: command not found" failure often means the runtime image does not include Maven; resolve it by installing Maven in the install phase or switching to a custom image with Maven preinstalled. If logs indicate "AccessDenied" when uploading artifacts, check the service role's S3 permissions. Debugging is iterative: update buildspec or image, re-run, and verify CloudWatch logs. Key takeaway: read the logs carefully, correlate timestamps and commands, and apply minimal fixes to isolate the real cause rather than broad sweeping changes. Troubleshooting CodeBuild failures means use cloudwatch logs to trace failing commands, then fix buildspec, environment, or iam role permissions as needed; iterate and re-run builds.. In practical terms, use cloudwatch logs and configuration checks to find root causes. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. Step-by-step debugging
  1. Open CloudWatch logs for the build run and find the failing timestamp.
  2. Read the failing command output and exit code to identify the error.
  3. Check buildspec syntax, artifact and cache paths, and runtime-versions.

screens.title: Assessment and common scenarios
screens.narratorSegment: This lesson presents two assessment scenarios that reinforce troubleshooting and configuration skills. Question one: a Java build fails in install with "mvn not found" even though runtime-versions: java:corretto11 is set. The likely cause is that the managed image does not include Maven by default. fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson we focus on AWS CodeBuild as a managed continuous integration service that compiles code, runs tests, and produces deployable artifacts. You will learn why designing the right build environment matters, how the buildspec. yml file controls each phase, and practical ways to speed up builds using caching and appropriate compute types. We will also show how CodeBuild fits into an automated pipeline and how to use CloudWatch logs and the service role to diagnose failures. A concrete example in this chapter walks through creating a simple Node. js project, adding a buildspec with caching for npm packages, running a build, then running it again to observe cache restoration. Along the way we call out common mistakes, such as using oversized base images or missing IAM permissions, and how to resolve them. By the end you should be able to choose between managed images or custom Docker images, author purposeful buildspec phases, and interpret logs to fix failing builds. Think about a recent build you ran slowly: which of the ideas here could speed it up or make failures easier to fix?

By the end of this chapter you will be able to design and implement custom build environments that match your tooling needs, author robust buildspec. yml files that define install, pre-build, build, and post-build phases, and apply caching and compute choices to improve build speed and cost. You will also integrate CodeBuild into automated pipelines and troubleshoot failures using build logs and service-role permissions. Each objective here targets practical skills: creating a custom Docker image to include proprietary tools, writing buildspec commands that capture test and artifact steps, choosing S3 or local caching to speed package installs, and reading CloudWatch logs to locate the exact failing command. These are hands-on, job-ready abilities that directly impact deployment reliability and developer feedback cycles. Think of an intermittent build failure you have seen: with these objectives you should be able to identify whether the issue stems from the runtime, missing tools, IAM permissions, or incorrect buildspec paths and then fix it.

This continuation reinforces the skills you'll practice and clarifies common pitfalls. You will learn to select between managed images and custom Docker images when your project requires non-standard tools. You will practice writing specific buildspec commands, including installing dependencies, running linters and security scans, and packaging artifacts. You will also test caching configurations and observe the difference between local and S3 caches, seeing how S3 supports shared caches across projects while local cache benefits single-project speed. Finally, you will debug builds by reading CloudWatch logs for command failures, checking service role permissions for S3, ECR, and CloudWatch, and iterating on the buildspec or Docker image. Each card here maps to hands-on milestones: build an image or adjust the install phase, enable caching and re-run builds, and resolve a permission-related failure. These are the routine tasks you will repeat daily as a DevOps professional.

AWS CodeBuild is a fully managed continuous integration service that compiles source code, runs tests, and produces artifacts ready for deployment. The core claim is that CodeBuild removes the need to provision and manage your own build servers by offering on-demand build capacity that scales automatically, so you pay only for build minutes consumed. A concrete example: a repository push triggers a pipeline, CodeBuild pulls the source, runs install commands, executes unit tests, and zips artifacts to S3 for later deployment. A common misconception is that CodeBuild alone handles orchestration; in practice, you typically integrate it into CodePipeline or other orchestrators to form a CI/CD workflow. Another misunderstanding is assuming every managed image contains every tool; you may need to install or supply a custom image for specialized tools. Key takeaway: CodeBuild handles execution and scaling, but you must define the commands, artifacts, and environment so that builds are reproducible and secure. Ask yourself: which repeating manual steps in your current builds could be codified into a buildspec so they run automatically every time? What is AWS CodeBuild? means codebuild runs builds in managed or custom environments, scaling compute and producing artifacts while you pay for build time only.. In practical terms, a managed ci service that runs builds and produces artifacts. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Choosing the right build environment is a practical trade-off. CodeBuild offers managed images for common runtimes like Node. js, Java, Python, and Docker, which simplify setup for standard projects. However, advanced projects often require pre-installed tools, specific compilers, or proprietary software; for those you provide a custom Docker image stored in Amazon ECR or Docker Hub. Custom images let you guarantee tool versions and reduce repeated install steps, but you must keep images lean to avoid longer startup times. A common mistake is using a large base image with unnecessary packages; prefer smaller bases such as slim or Alpine where feasible. Security matters: regularly scan custom images and build them from trusted sources. Example: if your build runs a proprietary static analysis tool, bake it into a custom image and push to ECR so CodeBuild can pull it during the build without additional install steps. Misconception to avoid: assume managed images include every build tool; always verify the managed image documentation and install missing tools in the install phase or via a custom image. How would you balance startup time and reproducibility in your project?

The buildspec. yml file is the heart of a CodeBuild project. It is a YAML document typically stored at the root of your repository that instructs CodeBuild what to do during each phase. The main phases are install for dependency installation, pre_build for checks like linting or security scans, build for compiling and unit tests, and post_build for packaging artifacts or pushing Docker images. You can also define artifacts to collect build outputs and cache. paths to persist dependency caches. A concrete example is a Node. js project that sets runtime-versions: nodejs: 18 in install and runs npm install, then runs tests in build and zips artifacts in post_build. A common mistake is incorrect paths in cache. paths or artifacts. base-directory, causing caches to miss or artifacts to be empty. When a build fails because a tool is missing, ensure the managed image supports the runtime or add installation commands to the install phase, or use a custom image. Close by asking: does your buildspec clearly separate environment setup from build steps so failures are easier to diagnose? Understanding buildspec.yml means author structured phases and declare artifacts and cache paths to make builds deterministic and fast.. In practical terms, phases, commands, artifacts, and cache. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Here we walk through the example buildspec. yml used for the Node. js hands-on activity. The file locks runtime-versions to nodejs: 18 in the install phase and runs npm install to restore dependencies. The build phase runs the build script and unit tests, while the post_build phase packages artifacts, such as zipping the app for S3 storage. Notice cache. paths includes /root/. npm so subsequent builds can restore node_modules from S3 and avoid downloading packages again. A practical mistake to watch for is using an incorrect cache path format; the pattern '/root/. npm/**/*' captures nested files and is commonly recommended. If caches are not found, check the CodeBuild project's cache configuration in the console, ensure the service role has s3:GetObject and s3:PutObject permissions, and confirm the bucket and prefix names match. This example is intentionally simple so you can run it, observe logs like "Restoring cache...", and then experiment by changing the cache path and re-running builds to see the effect. Example buildspec for Node.js means a practical buildspec locks runtimes, runs install/build/test, packages artifacts, and configures cache paths for faster repeat builds.. In practical terms, a complete buildspec.yml used in the hands-on activity. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Caching is one of the most effective levers to reduce build times. CodeBuild supports S3 caching, which is useful for larger caches that multiple projects share, and local caching, which is faster but scoped to a single build project. A concrete example: caching the node package store at /root/. npm lets subsequent builds skip re-downloading all dependencies. To enable caching you define cache. paths in buildspec. yml and configure the CodeBuild project's cache type to S3 or Local. If you pick S3, ensure the service role has s3:GetObject and s3:PutObject permission for the cache bucket. If you see "Cache not found" in logs, likely causes are incorrect cache paths, misspelled bucket names, or insufficient IAM permissions. Test caching by running a build twice: the first run creates the cache, and the second should show "Restoring cache..." and a faster install phase. Misconception: caching always speeds builds; in some cases a corrupt or stale cache may cause failures, so add cache invalidation strategies when dependencies change dramatically. What cache strategy best fits your environment: fast local restores for a single project, or S3 to share caches across teams?

CodeBuild offers a range of compute types with different C P U and memory characteristics. The right choice depends on your workload: a small static site build usually needs minimal C P U and memory and benefits from a smaller compute type, while large parallel test suites or container builds may require larger types like XLARGE. The primary trade-off is cost versus speed — oversized compute wastes money, while undersized compute can make builds slow or cause out-of-memory failures. A practical tip: profile a typical build run on a medium instance then measure whether C P U or memory is saturated; scale up only when the workload requires it. CodeBuild commonly serves as a build or test action inside an AWS CodePipeline stage. The pipeline provides orchestration: a source stage hands artifacts to CodeBuild, CodeBuild produces compiled artifacts or Docker images, and subsequent stages deploy or run additional tests. Security is enforced by the CodeBuild service role — an IAM role assumed during builds. This role needs least-privilege permissions to access sources (CodeCommit, S3, GitHub), S3 buckets for artifacts and cache, ECR for Docker images, and CloudWatch Logs. A frequent troubleshooting scenario is a permission-related failure: for example, a build cannot upload artifacts to S3 because the service role lacks s3:PutObject. To resolve this, inspect CloudWatch logs for permission-denied messages and update the service role policies accordingly. Misconception: granting overly broad access to the role may seem simple but increases attack surface. Always grant just the permissions the build requires. After integrating, run a pipeline and observe that builds are triggered automatically by source changes, producing artifacts that feed the next stages. Troubleshooting CodeBuild builds requires a methodical approach. The primary source of truth is CloudWatch Logs, which stream every command and its output. Start by locating the timestamp where the build stopped or where an error message appears, then inspect the failing command and its exit code. Common root causes include incorrect buildspec syntax, missing tools in the environment, incorrect cache or artifact paths, network failures to external resources, and insufficient IAM permissions for the service role. For example, an "mvn: command not found" failure often means the runtime image does not include Maven; resolve it by installing Maven in the install phase or switching to a custom image with Maven preinstalled. If logs indicate "AccessDenied" when uploading artifacts, check the service role's S3 permissions. Debugging is iterative: update buildspec or image, re-run, and verify CloudWatch logs. Key takeaway: read the logs carefully, correlate timestamps and commands, and apply minimal fixes to isolate the real cause rather than broad sweeping changes. The CodeBuild service role is central to builds interacting with S3, ECR, and CloudWatch Logs; always apply the principle of least privilege when granting permissions.
